title: Conflict Is Not the Problem, Silence Might Be
author: Meller Notes
summary: The piece argues that most leaders who consider themselves diplomatic or careful about picking battles are actually conflict-avoidant, letting known problems sit unaddressed because raising them feels harder than living with them, when in fact the cost of silence is almost always higher, just diffused across the whole team as an ongoing tax rather than concentrated in a single uncomfortable conversation. The author is careful to distinguish this argument from an endorsement of conflict as performance or venting, which they describe as genuinely corrosive, and instead names a narrower skill: 'conflict routing,' the discipline of taking a tension that would otherwise leak sideways into gossip and avoidance and moving it deliberately into the one conversation, with the one person, where it can actually be resolved. Central to the piece is the claim that most organizational silence isn't peaceful at all, it's conflict that has gone underground and become more damaging because it's invisible to the people who could actually resolve it. The piece closes by reframing the needed leadership skill as neither confrontation-seeking nor avoidance, but noticing where tension is currently leaking sideways and redirecting it into a closeable channel.
points: Distinguishes conflict-avoidance dressed up as diplomacy from genuine conflict-as-performance, arguing the former is much more common among leaders and much more costly than they realize.

Argues the cost of an unaddressed problem doesn't disappear when leaders stay silent, it moves from a visible, contained conversation to a diffuse, ongoing tax the whole team pays through behavioral adjustment.

Reframes organizational silence as conflict that has 'gone underground' -- gossip, eye contact, quiet recalibration of who gets invited to what -- arguing this is conflict fully present, just relocated somewhere unresolvable.
Names a specific, narrower leadership skill, 'conflict routing': noticing where tension is leaking sideways and deliberately moving it into the one conversation where it can actually be closed.
quotes: What they are actually doing, most of the time, is letting a known problem sit unaddressed because raising it feels harder than living with it.
It just moves the cost from a visible, contained conversation to a diffuse, ongoing tax on the whole team.
Conflict as performance, as venting, as a way to establish dominance, is genuinely corrosive, and leaders who mistake volume for honesty are not doing what I'm describing.
Most organizational silence isn't peaceful. It's just conflict that has gone underground, where it does more damage precisely because it's invisible to the people who could resolve it.
I think the actual skill leaders need is not conflict avoidance and it's not conflict-seeking. It's what I'd call conflict routing.
It's notice where a tension is currently leaking sideways, and move it, deliberately, into the one channel where it can be closed instead of just managed.
